catalog_quote: Songola language is given the Bantu classification number D.24 in Guthrie (1967) and is called also as "Binja nord" (namely North Binja, coupled with Zimba, or South Binja) by Meeussen (1951b manuscript; Bastin, 1975). ... All these are tone languages having principally a high tone and a low tone. Table 2 summarizes the linguistic traits of Songola and Bwari languages. In order to clarify the tones of the word, I asked the informants to add "my" (.ane/.ané in Songola, for example) to a noun. I asked an informant to reproduce the tones of Songola words with a wooden slit drum (lu.kumbí) and confirmed the tones. In this paper, high tones are marked with the symbol "´" whereas low tones are left unmarked. [Table 2A, tones:] High: /´/. Low: without tone marks, except for consonants having one mora such as /ḿ/ and /ń/.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. Songola (Enya, Kuko and Binja subgroups; D.24) is described as a two-tone language (H vs. L, lexical tone confirmed by frame-substitution and slit-drum reproduction); tone marking is used on all vernacular forms. Neither Ankei 1989 nor Ankei 1990 nor Jacobs & Omeonga 2001 mention stress or accent at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: the connective 'of' is generally high-toned but in classes 1, 4 and 9 the high tone falls on the next syllable (after Meeussen 1951b).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated nouns and fish names, with the possessive frame '.ane' used to check tones); phoneme and tone tables refer to the Songola-Enya dialect near Kindu, with notes on Binja and Kuko dialects. The author is an ethnobiologist, not a phonologist; the primary linguistic source he relies on is Meeussen's unpublished 'Notes Binja-N' (1951, Tervuren).
new_statements.identity_note: Songoora = Songola = Binja-Nord / North Binja (D.24), Kindu–Kailo area, Maniema. Ankei's data are from the Songola-Enya subgroup (villages Tongomacho/Elila near Kindu) with checks on Kuko and Binja subgroups; Jacobs & Omeonga describe Isiamba/Isilwamba (Tulungu, north of Lokandu), which Glottolog equates with sod. Delhaise 1909 'Wasongola du Sud (Bantu ba Bili)' probably belongs to the southern Binja/Zimba side (zimb1251) rather than Songoora proper. The Stuhlmann 1894 'Wassongora' are the Busongora of the Rwenzori area and are not this language.

new_statements.quote: La langue songola est classée en D-23 par Guthrie (1967) et appelée "binja-N" par Meeussen (1951 m.s.). Le bembe est semblable au songola, et tous deux ont sept voyelles /ɩ i e a o u ʋ/. [...] Toutes les langues citées sont tonales; elles ont un ton haut "´" et un ton bas "`". [p. 6] — Les tons des mots enya ont été relevés comme suit: Les informateurs ont été priés d'ajouter "mon" (-ané) à chacun des noms de poisson, ce qui a rendu les tons clairs et stables. L'emploi d'un tambour-signal à fente traditionnel (lùkúmbí) a facilité leur notation. [note 5, p. 41]
new_statements.translation: The Songola language is classified as D-23 by Guthrie (1967) and called "binja-N" by Meeussen (1951 ms.). Bembe is similar to Songola, and both have seven vowels /ɩ i e a o u ʋ/. [...] All the languages cited are tonal; they have a high tone "´" and a low tone "`". [p. 6] — The tones of the Enya words were recorded as follows: the informants were asked to add "my" (-ané) to each fish name, which made the tones clear and stable. The use of a traditional slit signal-drum (lùkúmbí) facilitated their notation. [note 5, p. 41]

new_statements.relation_note: Same finding as the existing statement from the 1989 English version of the same study (Ankei 1989, ASM Suppl. 9): tonal language with H and L, no statement on stress. The catalog record has an empty rule, consistent with 'tone language, no stress statement'. Adds nothing new on stress; confirms the tone-marking method (frame -ané, slit drum) also for the French text.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Songola (Enya subgroup, Kindu) is described as a two-tone language (high vs. low), with tones marked on every fish name; the article says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence (search of the full scanned text for accent, tonique, intensité, proéminence, prosodie, syllabe: no hits). The 'Langues' section is a half-page classification note, not a phonology section.
new_statements.exceptions: none; note that this French version gives Guthrie D-23 where the 1989 English version gives D.24 (D.24 is the correct Guthrie number for Songola)
new_statements.identity_note: Ankei 1986 describes the Songola of the Kindu area (Maniema), specifically the Enya fishing subgroup who speak Songola ('binja-N', Meeussen); the same population as Ankei 1989. Not the Zimba/South Binja (D.26) variety.

tone_statements.quote: Eigen kenmerken van het Lega-complex vinden we op het gebied van de klanken en de woordenschat, maar vooral in de spraakkunst. Phonologisch worden zeven klinkers onderscheiden, maar er is geen tegenstelling tussen korte en lange klinker, ook al wordt de klinker van de voorlaatste klankgreep regelmatig lang gerealiseerd. Het toonstelsel vertoont rechtstreeks verband tussen toon en element : „syllabische” toon zonder verdubbeling, verschuiving of omkering. Dit alles is hetzelfde als in talen gelijk het Mongo, maar verschillend van het Luba-complex (ook Bangubangu) en het Ganda-Rundi-complex (ook Furiiru), waar we vijf klinkers hebben en de tegenstelling tussen lange en korte klinker. [p. 388] — Kernen met eigen hoge toon hebben in bepaalde werkwoordvormen en in oneigenlijke adjectieven tooncontrast tegenover de voorafgaande klankgreep in de westelijke en noordelijke talen : Noord-Binja 4 yalúlúká, 11 lwáluluka rood [p. 389]
